doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Band turnover, being misjudged, and Frank Tiberi
summary: Turnover after the first record, his reluctance to criticize, differing views of him, and Frank Tiberi asking about his reed.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: There was a big, fairly significant turnover after the first Blood, Sweat & Tears record. Did that come internally or was that partly from like Columbia Records.

I don’t think they had anything to do with that. Look, I’m one-ninth. And I tell people, I’ve written stories about Blood, Sweat & Tears, little things, without putting anybody down because I just don’t want to do that. Because there’s different views. I’m not perfect you know. So there’s people that don’t like me as a teacher. They don’t like me because I’m a nice guy, they don’t like my smile. It’s just the way it is. You know, that’s the way it is. Other people think I’m the best piano player in the world, or, really, or at Berklee out of a lot of good piano players. And I never studied you know. Some good people. So it’s crazy. I’ve heard people say, “You play better than Charlie Parker.” And I don’t cry — I was playing a couple of years ago in a room and Frank Tiberi, who’s a great saxophone player. He’s 88, 89 years old now. He’s still bopping around. Plays really great, not modern, but we’re very friendly. And I think he was repairing my horn

or something but I was playing my alto and he was in another room down the hallway at Berklee. Everybody else was gone, it was nighttime. And he was nice enough to fix my horn or do something. So I was really up on playing my horn. I wasn’t playing all the time, but it just felt great. So I go into his room and I played a couple of notes, which he has rarely heard me play. And he said, I’m being silly now, but he says, “What kind of reed you got? What kind of mouthpiece you got?” I said, “Frank, it’s not the mouthpiece.” And he’s a great player. It’s like I play good. It’s not — it’s me. If I’m out of shape I might sound worse. But you should know that.
